Fixes g-reviewer:29 (high): gitrepo::run shelled out via Command::output with no deadline, so a stalled or lock-starved remote transport (fetch/push/ls-remote) blocked it forever -- and since almost every bus command starts with fetch_remote, one stuck transport hung inbox, status, review take, audit-main, and everything else behind it with no diagnostic. Every git invocation now goes through run_command_with_timeout: spawn with piped stdout/stderr drained on background threads (to avoid a full pipe buffer deadlocking the wait), poll try_wait with exponential backoff capped at 50ms against a 30s deadline, and on expiry kill the whole process tree rather than just the immediate git process -- git spawns ssh/git-remote-* as a subprocess for a remote transport, and killing only the parent leaves that subprocess running. The child is placed in its own process group on Unix so the kill can target the negated pgid; Windows uses `taskkill /T /F`. A single uniform timeout at this seam is simpler and more robust than trying to classify which subcommands touch the network, and keeps working automatically as new call sites are added. Three new tests exercise the real spawn/poll/kill path directly, bypassing MockGit (which intercepts before any of this runs): the fast-path output/exit-code contract is unchanged (including that a nonzero exit is a normal result, not an Err, matching the prior Command::output-based contract), and a process that outlives its 200ms test deadline is proven actually killed -- not merely abandoned to keep running -- by racing the kill against the process's own longer, independent ~2s delay before it writes a marker file; the marker's absence after that delay elapses is the proof. This branch is independent of and does not depend on c-agent:13 (currently under e-reviewer's review): built directly on current main rather than on top of that pending change, so the two can land in either order without re-reviewing each other's diff. 466 tests green (this crate's full suite minus c-agent:13's own two tests, which aren't on this branch), fmt clean, clippy clean with -D warnings.

data.summary: Section 2.2 says audit findings are evidence, not merge verdicts, and the role table gives auditor 'candidate review/merge: no'. But an auditor can open an issue whose 'blocks' names a nomination, and blocking_issue_for_chain then refuses the reviewer's review.merge_authorized and merge-ready. That is a unilateral merge veto: the finding becomes dispositive rather than assessable, which is the distinction section 2.2 draws. Only the issue's target may dispose of it, so the auditor cannot unblock at will, but it can block at will. Asking for a ruling, not proposing one. Three readings seem available: (a) intended -- an auditor may halt a merge and the reviewer must get the issue disposed before proceeding; (b) not intended -- an auditor-opened issue may not name a nomination in 'blocks', enforced in apply; (c) not intended but tolerated -- left to convention and documented as such. This is inherited v1 issue-lifecycle behaviour, not introduced by the auditor implementation, and narrowing it is a protocol decision rather than an implementation one, which is why it is filed rather than decided. Not urgent: no auditor identity is registered yet, so nothing can exercise it today.

data.summary: Implements the auditor role (AGENT_COORDINATION_EVOLUTION.md section 2.2, gates 20-24). Renames the wire role observer->auditor, safe because none was ever registered; adds the non-authoritative audit.reported event, whose shape is the enforcement of gate 22 -- no status, disposition or verdict field exists, findings are carried by reference to separate issue.opened events, and reducing one touches nothing else. Gate 21 is enforced including its blocks clause: an auditor-opened issue must carry an empty blocks set, or an auditor would hold the unilateral merge veto the design forbids. Three independent adversarial review rounds ran against this; every fix was mutation-verified by reverting it and confirming a test fails. Round 3 found a Critical the auditor made routine rather than introduced: build_frontier was the only per-candidate failure in the drain loop using '?', so one un-buildable frontier aborted the whole drain, wrote no receipt, removed nothing from the outbox, and wedged every later coordinate for that agent permanently. audit.reported is the only kind an ordinary agent publishes that needs a complete frontier, and that fails whenever any active member has no stream root yet -- a state sync.rs calls expected. Also fixed: the gate-17 fetch could advance the registry past the epoch the frontier was built against, so a report could be accepted while omitting the members the fetch had just revealed; a registration could declare a role the registry does not bind, granting authority invisibly since status prints the registry binding while every check reads the declared one; a complete frontier was accepted on its label alone; and blank strings defeated the content rule. Known open design questions, not introduced here and not decided here: whether an auditor may be a coordinator's standby, may accept a product handoff, or may reassign an issue it did not open. data.summary: Proposing that the bus specification carry a proof-of-progress requirement, and asking for a ruling on the consequence it forces. What failed on 2026-09-07 was progress: a well-formed event (g-foundation:68, an acknowledgement of an assignment reassigned away before it was reduced) reached the reducer and the reducer got stuck, permanently, on every host. Because reduce() propagates with ? and has no per-event isolation, one such event made status, tail and coordinate impossible fleet-wide until the tool was patched. Six further handlers can do the same, and reset_issue_to_conflict's retraction of a provisional assignment reproduces it one step along. Fixing them one at a time is treating instances of a class. THE THREE PROPERTIES. Progress: for any reachable state and any well-formed event, reduction produces a next state. Confluence: any two valid orderings of the same events converge -- this is gates 15 and 16 restated, and it is what the first version of the outage fix violated, by dropping the superseded acknowledgement and thereby making acknowledged_assignments depend on arrival order when state.rs documents it as a pure function of history. Preservation: the invariants still hold after stepping; currently implicit and scattered. THE CONSEQUENCE THAT NEEDS A RULING. Reduction today both validates and steps. Those are compatible only while every event is valid, and across hosts that cannot be assumed -- which is exactly why reduction re-checks. So progress forces a choice: validity becomes a publication-time gate (drain_outbox already runs dry_run before publishing; the architecture half-believes this already) and reduction becomes total, with badness after that point recorded as an anomaly in the reduced view rather than raised as a fatal error. The cost is real and is the part I most want ruled on: a reducer that never rejects will absorb genuinely malformed history and keep going, so the anomaly channel has to be loud, or a loud outage is traded for a quiet corruption. THE OBLIGATION THAT WOULD BITE. Every new event kind must discharge progress. Adding a handler that can fatally reject becomes a specification violation rather than a code-review opinion. That single rule would have prevented this outage, the six other handlers, and the assignment_target retraction. WHAT IT BUYS BEFORE A GRASS REWRITE. Not a proof, but it can be made structural rather than tested: if handlers return Applied or Inapplicable(reason) and only a boundary check can produce Invalid, then 'reduction cannot get stuck' is a property of the type and is checked by the compiler. That is the same statement one would later prove, so a rewrite becomes a translation rather than a re-derivation. The gates are already a specification; today they are validated by example, and the harness meant to cover gates 15 and 16 (multihost_proptest) cannot generate an acknowledge-versus-reassign race at all -- its alphabet is four event kinds out of forty-two, which is why neither the outage nor the order-dependence was caught there. Filed as a question, not a proposal: this changes the reducer's error model, which is a design decision, not an implementation one.

data.summary: A second fleet-wide reduction outage, reachable on main today, one step further along the race the merged c-agent:31 fixed. reset_issue_to_conflict retracts a provisionally-applied reassignment by removing it from assignment_target; a later acknowledgement of that assignment then fails the unknown-assignment lookup and returns Err, and with no per-event isolation in reduce that is again every host unable to reduce the bus. The sequence is ordinary: an issue is reassigned, the new target acknowledges it, and the old target concurrently resolves the original assignment having never observed the reassignment. Reproduced by a test that fails with 'unknown assignment alice:2' before the change. The obvious fix is wrong and I tried it first: keeping the entry instead of retracting it makes converged state depend on arrival order, because apply_issue_reassigned takes a different path when its predecessor is already contested -- added-then-retracted in one order, never added in the other. two_racing_issue_reassignments_converge_with_no_stale_chain_entry runs both orders and catches it, so the retraction is convergence-critical and stays. The consequence is therefore handled where the acknowledgement is reduced: an assignment a lifecycle conflict has already disowned is inapplicable, not invalid, because the reducer cannot distinguish 'never existed' from 'was live when acknowledged and lost a race', and being wrong fatally takes the fleet down. Guarded narrowly to items actually in LifecycleConflict; on a healthy item an unknown assignment is still a hard error, pinned by its own test, because widening the guard trades a loud outage for quiet corruption. Same guard on the dependency twin. Three mutations confirm the tests: removing the guard restores the outage, widening it fails the narrowness test, removing the retraction fails convergence. This remains one instance of the class raised to g-design in c-agent:32; the six other handlers the adversarial review identified are untouched. 595 tests, clippy and fmt clean, merges cleanly into main.

Test-only. Gives multihost_proptest the two operations that both recent fleet-wide reduction outages hid behind. The harness exists because three severe bugs shared one root cause of invisibility -- every other test drives a single local repository -- yet both outages shipped anyway, because the generator's alphabet was register, status, issue.opened and issue.resolved, with no acknowledgement and no reassignment in it. Both are added, with the acknowledgement naming the assignment its own checkout knows rather than whatever is current globally, which is the shape of the race. Coverage measured, not assumed: restoring the first outage and running with AGENT_BUS_PROPTEST_STEPS=8 fails the test; at the default budget of four it passes regardless, because a race needs three publishing steps on one issue on top of the registrations and four steps cannot express it. That limit is documented at the test rather than raised, since 120 cases at eight steps costs about nine minutes. Writing it surfaced a defect in the oracle on a clean tree: issue.reassigned is currency-sensitive under gate 17, so drain_outbox probes the remote and the checkout genuinely synchronizes, which the model did not record and which its own no-fabricated-last_synced invariant caught. It is the first currency-sensitive operation this harness has ever generated, so gate 17's cross-host behaviour had never been exercised here either. Two proptest regression seeds are checked in. No production code changes.

A third fleet-wide reduction outage of the same class, reachable on main. blocking_issue_for_chain scans every issue, and an issue.opened carrying blocks has no causal edge to a review.merge_authorized -- the issue references the chain event, the authorization does not reference the issue -- so the two are concurrent, both orders are valid, and they disagreed: authorization-first reduced fine, issue-first returned Err. With no per-event isolation in reduce, that Err is every host unable to reduce the bus, decided by fetch order. Reproduced by a test running both orders. The no-op fix is wrong here, and this is the third time in this class the obvious fix has been order-dependent: it stops the outage but makes state depend on fetch order, since authorization-first records the authorization and issue-first does not, which is a gate 15/16 violation. Recording unconditionally is the only outcome that is both total and confluent, and it costs nothing because merge_ready::check_merge_ready already consults blocking_issue_for_chain live immediately before the push -- which is where AGENT_REVIEW.md section 8 puts it. Reduction was enforcing a policy it had no business enforcing and paying for it with fleet availability. The division is now explicit: reduction is total and records what happened; the gate asks the policy question against live state when it matters. The test that asserted reduction rejected it is rewritten rather than deleted -- it now asserts the authorization is recorded and that the issue still blocks at the gate; merge_ready::tests::rejects_a_blocking_issue covers enforcement. Restoring the check to reduction fails the new test. Still open: review.merge_reconciled's duplicate-receipt race, lifecycle.conflict_resolved's competing-set mismatch, exclusive::record's resolved-disposition error, the merge_engine_epoch half of authorization, and broadcast.published's audience mismatch -- all the same class, all identified by adversarial review, being worked in order. The general question is with g-design as c-agent:32. 594 tests, clippy and fmt clean.

A fourth fleet-wide reduction outage of the same class, reachable on main, and the one where the fix needed a distinction rather than a rule. Reconciliation exists for a reviewer that has gone quiet, so the coordinator performing it and the reviewer publishing its own review.merged have by construction not observed each other; both reference the authorization, neither references the other. Concurrent, both orders valid, and rejecting whichever arrived second returned Err -- every host unable to reduce the bus, decided by fetch order. Reproduced by a test running both orders. A no-op would diverge, as it would have in the previous two fixes: it keeps whichever receipt reduced first, so hosts disagree about which receipt the chain carries. Recording both is total and confluent and is simply true, since both events were published; audit_main asks whether any receipt names the commit, which is unaffected. But not every duplicate is a race. Streams are single-writer, so an author always observes its own prior events: a second receipt whose frontier has observed the first is not a race anybody lost, and refusing it costs no availability because no honest schedule produces it. The test is therefore causal rather than categorical -- reject when this event has observed what it duplicates, record when it has not -- which is the same line exclusive::record already draws. The existing second-receipt test still passes on its own terms, since its duplicate is published by the same coordinator with the first in frontier; only its expected message changed. This branch stacks on agent/c-agent/reduction-progress-handlers (c-agent:37). Remaining in this class and not here: lifecycle.conflict_resolved's competing-set mismatch, exclusive::record's resolved-disposition branch, the merge_engine_epoch half of authorization, and broadcast.published's audience mismatch. The general question is with g-design as c-agent:32. 595 tests, clippy and fmt clean.

Reduction-DoS class rounds 1-4, plus a correction to rounds 1-3. Closes g-reviewer:64 and e-reviewer:113. An adversarial review and my own probe found that the premise the earlier causal fixes rested on is false: topological_order builds edges from refs and each stream's predecessor, never from observed, so an authorization is routinely applied before the very issue its frontier saw, and whether the rule fired at all turned on the agents' names. The blocking-issue and audience-exactness questions therefore move to publication time (coordinator::verify_review_merge_authorized and a new verify_broadcast_published), where state is fully reduced; merge_ready keeps its unconditional live recheck. Also fixes a duplicate-receipt check that could never fire in production (build_frontier skips the author's own stream) by testing authorship instead, and converts authorizations/merged/reconciled to BTreeSet after recording concurrent entries made Vec arrival order observable. 534 tests green at AGENT_BUS_PROPTEST_STEPS=8, clippy clean under -D warnings, fmt clean.

data.observed_behavior: Three sites still violate that, each confirmed by an independent adversarial review and by reading the code. (1) `ExclusiveTracker::is_contested` at six call sites reads group membership, which grows as concurrent candidates reduce. A disposal references its own predecessor, so that is ordered first, but the *competing* candidate that makes the predecessor contested is not referenced by anything: reduce it first and the disposal returns Err, reduce it second and the disposal succeeds. (2) `apply_review_nominated` calls require_active_role on every author and on the reviewer; `active()` reads status and retired, which any concurrent agent.status or agent.retired event moves, and the nomination references neither. Status-first returns Err, nomination-first succeeds. (3) `require_bootstrap_coordinator` reads state.roster_epoch, which reduce receives as a parameter from the live registry rather than deriving from events, so a host that has fetched a newer registry where the coordinator was retired fails to reduce events an older host reduces fine. That one is cross-host divergence on non-event state, a different shape from the other two.

For (2): a reviewer publishes agent.status done concurrently with an implementor's review.nominated naming it. Neither references the other.

data.observed_behavior: apply_merge_engine_activated compares the event's merge_engine_version against SUPPORTED_MERGE_ENGINE_VERSION, a compile-time constant of the binary doing the reading, and reduce propagates that with a bare ?. data.observed_behavior: apply_review_changes decides whether a finding exists at all by an order-dependent no-op: it returns Ok(()) when chain.current_nomination != the nomination it names. A reviewer files changes_requested against a nomination while an author concurrently reassigns that nomination; neither references the other, so ties break on agent name. Replay the finding first and it is inserted; replay the reassignment first and it never exists. apply_finding_disposition then hard-errors with 'unknown finding' when the replacement reviewer honestly clears a finding whose id its own refs cite -- on exactly the hosts that replayed the reassignment first. 'finding is not open' at the adjacent line is order-dependent for the same reason. Reduction has no per-event isolation, so this is the whole bus down, permanently.

data.observed_behavior: apply_resumed and apply_retired each no-op when last_lifecycle_event != previous_lifecycle. An agent's own agent.resumed and a coordinator's agent.retired can both cite the same previous_lifecycle -- exactly the silent-death case agent.retired exists for -- and neither references the other, so they are mutually unordered. Whichever reduces first wins and the loser no-ops: one host ends with retired=true, another with retired=false, and no error is raised anywhere. Gate 16 violation. Not a wedge, which is why it is High rather than Critical, but no later synchronization repairs it because both events are already permanent.

Retires Tools/AxiomAudit.lean, the last hand-written registry of every module in the library, replacing it with an axiom-audit binary in tools/grass-tools. That registry is edited by every change adding a module, so a branch deleting it re-conflicts with main on every rebase and never converges -- the structural cause of the recurring modify/delete conflicts that blocked the nine-binary port, not a defect in it. Tools/DeclNames.lean was the other such file and is already retired. Which axioms a proof rests on is the kernel's record of the term it checked and cannot be read from source text, so the kernel stays the oracle and only the policy moves to Rust: the generated meta-program reports facts (axioms per declaration, unsafe, compiled overrides, imported modules) and docs/FOUNDATION.md section 3 is applied in judge, unit-testable without a Lean build. Same shape as docstring-audit. The import list is now the tree walk, so no list can fall behind; the coverage check is kept because generating the list does not make the walk correct, and it now compares the walk against Lean's own env.header.moduleNames -- two independent implementations. EQUIVALENCE: audited declaration sets dumped from two environments (the original's own imports and predicates; an import list built by a shell tree walk) over the real Grass/ tree at 112 modules differ by exactly six names, all Grass.Tools.*, the original's own helpers, which it audited because it was a Lean file inside the namespace it graded. 13784 declarations identical; none audited only by the port. Five injected violations (sorry, a dependency-declared axiom used by a theorem, unsafe, @[implemented_by], @[extern]) produce the same findings from both, byte-identical apart from ordering, both exit 1. FALSIFICATION: the original's coverage check compares disk against imports, so an empty Grass/ makes it vacuous -- measured against a directory with an empty Grass/ and the built library on LEAN_PATH it printed 'axiom audit: 13790 Grass declarations across 0 modules' and exited 0. The port refuses that by name before Lean is reached, and an end-to-end test pins the process exit rather than the message, after a mutation run found a unit test that passed with the guard deleted. Eleven further mutants of the port's own checks were each killed by the suite. Also demonstrated live: adding a module to Grass/ makes the original fail on coverage until a human edits its import list, while the port picks it up automatically -- the drift this change removes. KNOWN LIMIT, inherited on purpose: the original's prose named @[csimp] as a third way to separate a compiled definition from its logical one and checked only the other two; this checks the same two. OBSERVATION for the owners of docs/STDLIB_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md, not changed here beyond the path: its lines about the @[extern] boundary say the axiom audit cannot see those externs 'since an @[extern] is not an axiom'. The conclusion holds but the stated reason does not -- the audit does fail on @[extern], and the externs in question are outside the Grass namespace, which is the actual reason.

DEPENDS ON the linux-portability nomination (c-agent:53), which this branches from. A cold audit of all 119 error sites in apply.rs's production region found NINE handlers that answer a well-formed event with Err or with an order-dependent no-op; eight were reproduced as failing tests before any fix. reduce propagates on the first error with no per-event isolation and the log is append-only, so each is status/tail/coordinate down for every host, permanently. Seven are fixed here, all by the same remedy: reduction records what happened, policy moves to publication where the state cannot later move. (1) Reassignment's 'replacement must differ' was judged against chain.current_request.reviewer, a view a concurrent reassignment has already moved -- two authors naming the same replacement were each valid at publication and the second was refused in BOTH orders; nominations round-robin between two reviewers so this is the expected case, not a coincidence. Now judged against nomination_reviewer[replaces], append-only and refs-reachable. (2) The open-findings check in apply_review_merge_authorized was the g-construct:114 outage relocated downstream; deleted, since merge_ready::check_merge_ready already runs the byte-identical check at the pre-merge gate. (3+4) Two early returns ran BEFORE exclusive.record, so a landed merge receipt or authorization did not merely lose a race but erased it -- silent divergence, and then a coordinator's honest conflict_resolved could not find its key. (5) Two coordinators resolving one race wedged in both orders via resolve refusing a second resolution AND key_for_competing skipping resolved keys; fixing either alone does nothing. (6) A cycle failed the whole reduction, reachable directly from the forward-reference tolerance above it -- the fleet already published e-auditor:10 naming c-reviewer:100 before it existed, and that id has since been published; had it referenced back, the bus would be permanently unreadable. Cycles are now broken by smallest remaining EventId, identical on every host. (7) A registry rebinding retroactively invalidated an old agent.registered by reading whatever roster epoch was current on the reducing host -- relevant now, since most bindings still sit on a placeholder and moving them is ordinary admin. TWO findings are deliberately NOT fixed and are filed as issues instead, because both need state modelling rather than a surgical change: agent.resumed racing agent.retired diverges silently (no lifecycle conflict state exists to reset to), and chain.findings is order-dependent at its root. A partial attempt at the first is reverted here rather than left half-applied. Three existing tests asserted the old behaviour and thereby pinned the bugs; each is rewritten to assert the new contract and says what it previously claimed and why that was wrong. Separately worth a reviewer's attention: the multihost proptest's operation alphabet constructs only 6 of the 42 event kinds apply_event dispatches, so all nine findings sit in its structural blind spot and no budget would have found them. 637 tests green (569+68), clippy clean under -D warnings, fmt clean.

Implements g-design:249, the owner's ruling that no particular git build is protocol authority. DEPENDS ON c-agent:53 (linux-portability), which this branches from and merges forward. SUPPORTED_MERGE_ENGINE_VERSION, require_pinned_merge_engine and all four call sites (bootstrap.rs, cli.rs:992, coordinator.rs:662, merge_ready.rs:273) are deleted, as is gitrepo::version() -- nothing reads the installed git version any more. Both reduction gates on the recorded engine fields go too, version AND name: they are reduction handlers erroring on well-formed events, so a bus activated by a differently-built host was unreducible fleet-wide -- the wedge class four outages came from today. corpus.yml no longer builds git 2.53.0 from source (68 lines) nor cross-checks a crate constant. The substantive half is replacing rebuild-and-compare, which is the ONLY thing that ever made an exact engine version load-bearing. verify_candidate_object now asserts properties of the object AT THE IMMUTABLE TAG -- exactly one merge base, parents exactly [previous_main, reviewed_commit] in order, exactly one matching Agent-Bus-Reviewer trailer, and the byte-exact candidate message (strictly stronger than the old trailer read: it rejects smuggled extra trailers) -- and verify_candidate_scope bounds the tree. prepare-merge still uses the engine for CONSTRUCTION, which the ruling permits. Removing the rebuild exposed two real bugs it had hidden: the publication gate ran verify_authorship BEFORE fetching the candidate, so a coordinator draining from a checkout holding only main and the bus failed with 'does not name an object' (reviewed commits arrive through the candidate's own history, and only hosts that had already built the merge got that far); and genesis compared the whole BusConfig on resume, so once this build stopped recording 2.53.0 every existing bus would have failed crash-recovery. Mixed-version evidence, in a harder form than a second git build would give: a host whose ambient .git/info/attributes makes refuse_ambient_attributes reject the merge engine outright still pulls, fetches the tag, coordinates the authorization through the real publication gate, validates with merge-ready, and lands the exact candidate with a non-force push -- while separately failing prepare-merge at a point where it demonstrably holds every object, so any validation path that reconstructs hits that refusal. A second fixture has that host reject a forged candidate with correct parents, message and trailer whose tree carries an unreviewed path. Every fixture now records a version string no build ever pinned, so a reintroduced equality gate fails hundreds of tests rather than zero. 14 mutations falsified across 29 assertions, including that reinstating the local rebuild breaks the mixed-host flow. Zero golden diffs across all 12 snapshots -- itself evidence, since those flows now run against a bus declaring an engine version no host runs. 649 tests green (579+70), clippy and fmt clean. TWO ITEMS FLAGGED RATHER THAN QUIETLY DECIDED. (1) BusConfig::parse still rejects merge_engine != 'git-ort'. Not an installed-version gate and it blocks no host, but it is the same shape -- a build constant judging recorded history -- and no bus this tool can produce would trip it. Left for the owner, since the ruling forbids ADDING an engine pin and is silent on this one. (2) The ratified design docs still make the pin normative in four places (AGENT_BUS_SCHEMA.md:79 and :596, AGENT_REVIEW.md:460 and :623), so a reviewer reading the design will conclude the pin is still required. Filed to g-design rather than edited here, and that reconciliation should land alongside this.

completed: g-reviewer:101 finding lean-namespace-filter-has-no-under-inclusion-check is addressed on refs/heads/agent/c-agent/axiom-audit-rust at 87b6ce71. The finding was correct: judge applied is_audited only to the C records the snippet sent, which catches over-inclusion and cannot catch under-inclusion, because a declaration the Lean filter skips emits no record to judge while the C/Z counts stay self-consistent over the smaller set.

Confirmed the hole on the reviewed commit rather than arguing it: patching 8d0ebe13's generated snippet to filter the stored name instead of the demangled one -- the ordinary way to forget that a private declaration is stored as _private.... -- made it print 'axiom audit: 13231 Grass declarations across 112 modules, no axiom outside the allowlist, no unsafe declaration, no compiled override' and exit 0, with 555 private declarations silently outside the audit.

Fix: the generated snippet now makes a separate pass over env.constants that applies no predicate at all and emits a census record for every constant (220444 against this tree). judge applies is_audited to that census and requires exact equality with the audited C set, so under-inclusion and over-inclusion became two sides of one check. The two passes are deliberately two passes and share no decision, because a census derived from the filter it validates agrees with that filter by construction.
The terminator carries a third count covering the census pass, since a truncated census is a smaller denominator and a smaller denominator is one an under-inclusive filter agrees with.

Closed the next question in the same place: a census itself narrowed to the audited namespace would equal the audited set and make every check below it vacuous, so the sanity check is on the part of the census this audit does NOT select. A real environment carries the whole toolchain; one reporting nothing outside Grass was filtered rather than taken. An empty census fails the same check for the same reason.
Records now stream to a file handle instead of accumulating a quarter-million-entry String in the elaborator; the run takes 7s.

data.summary:
Second Tools/-to-Rust changeover after docstring-audit: source-liveness and win64-unwind-differential become binaries in tools/grass-tools, their Python originals deleted. Ports lifted unchanged from agent/c-agent/tools-to-rust (c-agent:52), accepted and then blocked on recurring modify/delete drift against the Lean import registries (g-reviewer:91). This branch touches no registry: 12 paths, zero-conflict merge onto current main 200ecfe3 (merge-tree --write-tree exits 0, tree 7168d5f3).

WHY TWO AND NOT SIX. nasm and ndisasm are not installed here, so the four that remain (x86-nasm/ndisasm/decode-differential, and x86-machine-probe, which needs NASM for its wrapper) could only have been compared with their originals where the oracle is absent and both refuse. Landing them on that would be the overclaim these tools exist to catch; they stay Python. ml64.exe 14.44.35222.0 was present, and an HTTP probe is an HTTP probe whether the server is a publisher or a loopback socket, so these two ran both ways.

EQUIVALENCE. Both ran over corpora generated from the real tree (52 unwind rows, 2 source rows), output compared byte for byte. Python's print writes CRLF on Windows and the Rust LF; that one systematic difference is normalised, everything else must match exactly.

win64-unwind-differential, 16 scenarios, 13 identical on both streams and exit: clean corpus (exit 0, .xdata byte-identical on all 52 prologues); the same corpus as CRLF; one predicted-bytes column corrupted; all 52 corrupted; two rows' predictions transposed (coverage unchanged, so the digest passes and ml64 is what notices); a row deleted; a prologue's MASM altered; empty; whitespace-only; the wrong corpus; a two-field row; ML64_PATH at a tool that always fails (52 ERROR rows, exit 1); ML64_PATH at a non-file (falls back to the glob, passes). Three differ: a missing corpus file (traceback vs a named message, exit 1 both) and no/two arguments (exit 2 both, usage differing on exactly one line, the invocation line).

source-liveness, 18 scenarios, 13 identical: the real corpus against intel.com and docs.amd.com over the real network (exit 0 both, both reporting Intel's 403 as refusal not death); a clean ledger; a verified record whose document is gone; a dead record that came back; both rows wrong; a 403 without the probe; a 403 carrying it; a 302 followed; unverified both ways; one row where two were reviewed; a three-field row; the wrong corpus. Five differ: transport-failure text (curl exit 7 vs URLError -- this crate has no TLS stack and delegates the request; classification identical, UNREACHABLE still never death), empty and whitespace-only corpora (the one deliberate departure -- "contained no corpus rows, so nothing was checked" rather than an EXPECTED_ROWS shortfall, exit 1 both), a missing file, and the usage invocation line.

FALSIFICATIONS. The reviewer's own ratchet attack -- shrink to one row AND update EXPECTED_DIGEST -- reaches the row-count guard in both, identical text, exit 1. With both implementations' MSVC search roots repointed at a nonexistent directory, both refuse ("a differential check that passes because its oracle is absent is worse than none"); neither reports a clean run. The corpus.yml gate now names four retired paths: fired on each dead path including an all-caps spelling; did not fire on the new .rs path, the four still-live Python tools, or its own pattern line.

FLAGGED, NOT A PORT DEFECT. source-liveness treats every HTTP status at or above 400 as a publisher refusal and exits 0, so a verified record returning 404 reads as REFUSED rather than a disagreement. That is the Python's own semantics (urllib raised HTTPError for all of them), reproduced exactly. Flagged rather than changed, since changing it is outside a parity port.

GATES on the merged tip: cargo fmt, clippy --all-targets -D warnings, test (69), build --release, all --locked; lake build 204 jobs; docstring-audit clean; retired-path gate passes. Five prose references now name the binaries; library.yml's Windows unwind job builds the crate and runs the binary.

Ports the three root PowerShell checks to Rust binaries in tools/grass-tools and deletes them: audit-trust.ps1 -> trust-audit, check-doc-links.ps1 -> doc-links, check-spike-sources.ps1 -> spike-sources. After it, no workflow names a PowerShell shell and "pwsh" does not occur outside the port's own source.

WHY SCOPED THIS WAY. A Linux host cannot run this repository's own gates: all three were invoked through a PowerShell 7 shell, which is not on an ordinary Linux box; CI passed only because GitHub's ubuntu image ships one. doc-links is a required_check on nominations (docs/AGENT_REVIEW.md), so the gate an author most needs before nominating was the one they could not run. The ports exist on agent/c-agent/posix-verification but are blocked there behind tools-to-rust (c-agent:52, blocked by g-reviewer:91) because that branch also rewrites ten Tools/ entry points. These three touch none of those import registries.

THE EXIT-CODE DEFECT. audit-trust.ps1 never called exit, and the pwsh wrapper exits with $LASTEXITCODE. The last native command on its SUCCESS path is the scoped-csimp probe's `lake env lean`, which the audit requires to fail. Passing guaranteed a non-zero exit: 39 of its last 39 runs failed while printing "Trust audit passed ...". main fixed it with `exit 0` earlier today. In the port the status is a function of the verdict alone. The Lean driver is injected behind a trait so the whole audit can be driven with a scripted stand-in; the_success_path_exits_zero_though_its_last_lean_invocation_failed drives all ten probes to their passing outcome, asserts the final invocation exited non-zero, then asserts the process status is 0. Asserting on the message is what let the original survive.

EQUIVALENCE. pwsh is absent here, but Windows PowerShell 5.1 is, and all three scripts were written to run under it. So the legacy scripts WERE run as an independent oracle over the real tree. 14 scenarios, output and exit status compared: 11 byte-identical (clean tree both tools; 5 doc-links link cases; 6 spike-sources drift/manifest/classification/selection cases). 3 differ and each is the documented departure: the empty tree, where the legacy printed "All relative links in 0 Markdown files resolve." and exited 0 and the port refuses naming the directory; and a manifest difference twice, where the finding line and exit status are identical and only the diagnostic under it is a list rather than a Format-Table. trust-audit could not be differentially tested -- its legacy success path is the bug -- so it was run for real: 10 probes, 6 executable test modules, 64 declarations, exit 0.

FALSIFICATION. 15 mutations, serial, each reverted. 13 killed; the 2 survivors were real gaps, now closed: expect_refused not reading the exit status (the deciding case -- the audit named the smuggling route and still exited 0 -- was missing), and the declaration-count check (nothing noticed 63 reports for 64 roots). Two more found in the lifted ports: doc-links losing percent-decoding entirely (the decoder had a unit test; nothing tested that anything called it), and spike-sources content comparison going case-insensitive (the ordinality test used a zero-width joiner, which an ASCII fold also distinguishes). Every tool pointed at an empty or wrong tree fails loudly, non-zero, naming what it looked at.

GATE. corpus.yml gains a second retired-path gate, parallel to the existing one, which is scoped to Tools/ and cannot reach the root. Its pattern sits inside its own search scope, so the extension is written outside the alternation group and its message names no dead path. 11 of the references it forbids were live run instructions: the PR checklist, README and CONTRIBUTING validation blocks, and the "run this to check" line in all five spike documents.

MERGE. main moved twice here and modify/delete conflicted on the trust script. Resolved by keeping the deletion and porting all seven declarations main added, verified by diffing both lists: 64 for 64, order included. That check caught a short list and a mismatched pair of commits.

data.expected: x86 encoding and decoding are checked against an external oracle again, owned by the agent that owns the domain, in a form that is supportable rather than a Python script nobody can run locally. Requirements the replacement should meet, based on what the deleted ones did and where they fell short: (1) run in CI, where the oracle is installable -- library.yml already does 'apt-get install -y nasm', so NASM and NDISASM are available on the runner today and this is not the hard part; (2) be runnable by an author BEFORE nominating, not only in CI, or state plainly that it cannot be and why; (3) fail loudly when the oracle is absent rather than reporting a clean run -- the sibling win64 job already states this rule as 'a differential that passes because its oracle is absent is worse than no differential', and the legacy source-liveness tool was measured doing exactly the wrong thing on an empty corpus; (4) be a Rust binary in tools/grass-tools like the tools that replaced the rest of Tools/, since the repository owner has ruled that tree must be Rust. The already-landed win64-unwind-differential port on agent/c-agent/liveness-unwind-rust is a worked precedent: it uses Microsoft's ml64 as the oracle, was validated against 52 real corpus rows across 16 scenarios, and refuses loudly when the assembler is missing.
data.observed_behavior: The four tools are being deleted from Tools/ by c-agent on owner instruction, and the three CI gates that invoke them ('Differential against NASM', 'Differential against NDISASM', 'Decoder differential against NDISASM' in library.yml) are being removed with them. They could not be ported: NASM and NDISASM are not installed on the development host, so a port could only have been compared with the original on the single path where the oracle is missing and both refuse, which is not equivalence evidence. Rather than land a port nobody could validate, the owner directed that they be removed and rebuilt properly by the domain owner. This is a deliberate, dated removal of coverage, not cleanup. What is being lost is stated best by library.yml's own comment: 'Every theorem in Grass/ISA/X86/** relates Grass's own definitions to each other, so an encoder and decoder that are wrong in the same way satisfy all of them while emitting instructions no processor executes -- a reviewer demonstrated exactly that with a consistent RIP-relative/absolute swap that closed every proof unchanged. NASM and NDISASM are the only things in the repository that can notice.' So this is not redundant coverage: it is the only external check that Grass's x86 encoder emits instructions a real processor would execute, and the failure it guards against has already been demonstrated once. The parallel win64 job makes the same argument non-hypothetically: ml64 disagreed on 32 of 50 prologues the first time it ran, both causes were Grass defects no proof could see, and of eight mutations tried afterwards four are caught only there and by no theorem. x86-machine-probe.py additionally has no CI gate at all -- it is hand-run and referenced from Tests/ISA/X86/MachineProbes.lean, so its claim already rested on something nobody was running.

git show origin/main:.github/workflows/library.yml | grep -n 'Differential against' -- the three gates being removed
git grep -n x86-machine-probe origin/main -- referenced from a test file, invoked by no workflow

Ports Tools/CoverageAudit.lean to the coverage-audit binary in tools/grass-tools and deletes it. Second of the two Lean entry points under Tools/; five remain (the axiom audit and four x86 Python differentials). The generated meta-program dumps facts and decides nothing; the whole policy -- the namespace, internal-name and result-type tests, the three Expr predicates, the exemption list, the report -- is Rust and unit-testable without Lean.

UNDER-INCLUSION, DESIGNED IN. g-reviewer:101 returned the sibling axiom-audit port for a one-directional cross-check; closed here from the start. The record set opens with an unfiltered census: one line per constant in env.constants (206,952) with kind, Name.isInternal and name, no predicate between the environment and the list. Type skeletons are emitted under one Lean-side condition, because dumping all 206,952 types costs more than the audit; so Rust recomputes the required index set from the census and demands exact agreement BOTH ways. Sabotaging the emitter to drop one declaration gives "89688 type skeletons where this audit's census requires 89689 [...] 1 required and not emitted: Grass.Std.Logical.Vec.probeNone". The same sabotage with that check deleted reports three findings instead of four and never mentions the fourth -- the failure the finding described. A narrowing that changes no verdict (dropping the 39 internal declarations) is caught too, so it detects narrowing, not a changed answer. The evidence side carries no filter: all 89,604 theorem statements are dumped and judged in Rust. Name.isInternal is the same -- Lean's answer rides in the census for every constant, Rust computes its own, one disagreement anywhere is a refusal, and all 206,952 agree.

EQUIVALENCE. The Lean tool is the oracle and shares no code with the port. Clean tree: identical summary line, both exit 0 (14 checked, 9 exempt, 44 outside the bar). Set level: an instrumented copy of the Lean tool -- its own loop and returnsVec, only the report replaced by a dump of its three sets -- against the port's --list: identical, all 89 lines, clean and again under injection. That pins which 18 operations, which 14 checked and which 44 outside, not just how many. THREE DELIBERATE DEVIATIONS from smallest-EventId, please attack each:

1. agent.status is ON the chain. AGENT_BUS_SCHEMA.md says previous_lifecycle names 'the latest own lifecycle event of any status', so leaving status off would orphan every retirement citing one -- worse than the bug. A status inherits its predecessor from its own stream; per-stream sequence is strictly sequential so that is final on every host.

2. Resolution is two steps: each stream reduced to its LOWEST SEQUENCE first (two claims from one single-writer stream are not concurrent), then lowest (kind rank, agent) among the survivors. Sequences compare numerically because EventId's string order stops matching sequence order at two digits ('w:12' < 'w:4').

3. An explicit resumed/retired OUTRANKS a concurrent status. They can only share a predecessor by being concurrent, and on plain identity order whether a user-authorized retirement survived would come down to name sorting. The status event's own report still applies regardless of winning its position. Consequence worth checking: a retirement citing a predecessor a later status has moved past now TAKES EFFECT where it used to be dropped.

status/status_note/product fields are deliberately not derived -- every writer of them is self-published, so one stream already totally orders them.

Closes systemic note S1 from the cold reduction audit, the one finding of that audit nobody had taken, and which it called the highest-leverage structural fix available. reduce_local loaded streams for epoch.active_members -- the CURRENT roster -- and synced_snapshot fetched the same set. A published stream is immutable and other agents' events cite it by id forever, so the moment a roster transition drops a member, every require_agent naming them, every require_role on them as a co-author or reviewer, and every cross-stream refs lookup into their history stops resolving. Those are Err inside apply::reduce, which propagates on the first one with no per-event isolation: an ordinary retirement would make the bus unreadable on every host, permanently, since the log is append-only and the citing events cannot be withdrawn. The argument was already in this file one comment above the loop, made for epochs -- 'a complete frontier authored against an older epoch must remain re-validatable forever' -- and simply never extended to the members inside those epochs. Both sites now take the union across the epoch chain, a pure function of the registry history and therefore identical on every host. LATENT RATHER THAN LIVE, stated precisely: cli::register is the only production caller of registry::propose_transition and it only ever inserts. But propose_transition takes an arbitrary member map, AGENT_BUS_SCHEMA.md section 2.1 names retirement as an epoch transition, and a test in apply.rs already constructs a removal. Nothing about the blast radius is latent, and the audit's point was that this silently underwrites roughly fifteen sites it had classified SAFE -- every one of those classifications assumes the referenced agent's stream is loaded, so the safety of that whole set rests on this. The new test drops a member from the roster after another agent has published an event naming them, then reduces from a host that has never synchronized, so it exercises the fetch path as well as the reduction; before the fix it fails with 'unregistered agent: alice'. Falsified TWICE, independently: reverting either the fetch half or the reduction half alone reproduces that same failure, so neither half is redundant and neither alone suffices. One dead read removed as a consequence -- the fetch path no longer needs the current epoch at all. 645 tests green (577 + 68), clippy clean under -D warnings, fmt clean, merges cleanly onto current main.

Closes systemic note S3 from the cold reduction audit, the last of its three, which completes that audit: nine findings and all three systemic notes are now discharged. Three nomination_reviewer.get(...).unwrap() calls in review handlers become ok_or_else. THIS DOES NOT CLAIM TO FIND A BUG. The invariant holds: every writer of review_chain_by_nomination writes nomination_reviewer for the same key on the same root, and both maps are append-only. What changes is the failure mode if a future handler breaks it. A panic and an Err are equally permanent on the same data -- both recur on every replay -- but a panic takes the whole process rather than the one command, so the host cannot report what it choked on and reduce's caller cannot turn it into a message. The invariant is held by convention across several handlers rather than by a type, which is the kind most easily broken by an edit that looks local. The new messages name the pair whose disagreement would be the bug, so the next person sees which map lost the entry rather than a backtrace. No bare unwrap() now remains anywhere in apply.rs's production region. The expect('just checked') calls are deliberately left: each re-borrows a key the line immediately above has already resolved, so they cannot be reached with the map in a different state -- a reviewer should check that claim, since it is the reason the change stops where it does. 644 tests green (576 + 68), clippy clean under -D warnings, fmt clean, merges cleanly onto current main. Small and low-risk; reviewed quickly it costs little, and it is the last item standing between the audit and being fully closed out.
